name: Drones for Agricultural Monitoring 3: Crop Health, Pests and Data Processing
objectives: Given an NDVI or colour crop health map, read the legend and find the weak and strong zones, comparing differences within the field and with earlier maps
Given map patterns in a field, describe what each pattern may point to, such as pests, disease, water, machines or nutrients, treating each pattern as a clue to confirm, not a diagnosis
For each problem zone on a map, write a ground-truthing plan and record what you find at the spot, with zone number, coordinates, what you saw, likely cause, how sure you are and photos
Given a set of overlapping drone photos, stitch them into an orthomosaic with free software and check it for holes and blur, with the photos named, backed up and the result checked
Using QGIS and a multispectral orthomosaic, calculate and colour an NDVI map with the field boundary and ground points shown, using the formula (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red)
After ground-truthing, write a one-page field action report for the farmer, with a map picture, findings, a next step for each zone and who to contact, and no pesticide advice from the map

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Reading an NDVI crop health map
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Read an NDVI map using its colour scale and find the weak and strong zones.
This lesson builds toward: Given an NDVI or colour crop health map, you will read the legend and find the weak and strong zones, comparing differences within the field and with earlier maps.
NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) compares near-infrared and red light reflected by plants. Values run from -1 to +1. FAO explains that high positive values suggest dense, healthy vegetation, while low or negative values suggest sparse cover, bare soil or water.
On a drone NDVI map, each pixel gets a colour from a scale, often red for low values to green for high. Always read the legend: colours are relative to that map. A field that is all red early in the season may just be small plants and bare soil.
Look for differences within the field, not the colour alone. A low patch in an otherwise even maize field is worth a visit. Compare with earlier maps of the same field: a patch that is growing week after week matters more than one that stays the same.
Step by step:
- Read the legend: which colour is low and which is high?
- Note the crop and growth stage: young crops show more soil.
- Look for patches that differ from the rest of the field.
- Compare with an earlier map: is the patch new or growing?
- Mark the zones to visit.
Words to know:
- NDVI: a vegetation index from -1 to +1; higher usually means denser, healthier green plants.
- Legend: the key that shows what each colour on a map means.
- Growth stage: how far the crop has developed, from seedling to harvest.
Official sources:
- FAO GIEWS Earth Observation (NDVI and vegetation indicators)
Try it now: Find a sample NDVI map online (search for an NDVI map of a maize field) or use one of your own. Read the legend, mark two weak zones and one strong zone, and write what growth stage the crop might be at.
You can now read an NDVI map's legend and find the weak and strong zones worth visiting.

check.q: What does a high positive NDVI value suggest?
check.why: High positive NDVI values suggest dense, healthy vegetation; low values suggest sparse cover, soil or water.

check.q: A maize field is even green except for one low patch. What do you do?
options: Mark the patch to visit and compare it with earlier maps
Ignore it because most of the field is green
check.why: A low patch in an otherwise even field is worth a visit, and earlier maps show whether it is growing.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Spotting early pest, disease and stress patterns
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Recognise the map patterns that point to pests, disease, water or nutrient problems.
This lesson builds toward: Given map patterns in a field, you will describe what each pattern may point to, such as pests, disease, water, machines or nutrients, treating each pattern as a clue to confirm, not a diagnosis.
Different problems leave different shapes on a map. Patches that start small and spread outward over weeks can point to pests or disease, such as fall armyworm in maize or virus diseases in cassava. Problems along one edge may come from a neighbour's field, a road or wind. Straight stripes usually follow people or machines: a skipped fertilizer row, a blocked irrigation line, a planter fault.
Low, wet corners and dips point to waterlogging; high, sandy or sloping ground to water stress, especially on thermal images in the afternoon. Even yellowing across a whole field can point to a nutrient shortage such as nitrogen, but also to drought.
A pattern is a clue, not a diagnosis. Diseases and pests look alike from the air, and the treatments are very different. Fall armyworm sightings can be recorded with FAO's FAMEWS app where it is in use; confirm any suspected pest or disease with an extension officer or plant clinic before acting.
Words to know:
- Pattern: the shape and spread of a problem on a map: patch, edge, stripe, low spot.
- Fall armyworm: a caterpillar pest that eats maize and other crops; it spread across Africa from 2016.
- Plant clinic: a place where trained staff diagnose plant problems brought by farmers.
Official sources:
- FAO: mobile application to support the fight against Fall Armyworm in Africa (FAMEWS)
Try it now: Draw four small sketches of a field: one with a spreading patch, one with a problem along an edge, one with stripes, one with a low wet corner. Under each, write two possible causes.
You can now recognise common problem patterns on a crop map and list the likely causes to check.

check.q: What can a patch that starts small and spreads outward over weeks point to?
check.why: Patches that spread outward over weeks can point to pests or disease such as fall armyworm or cassava viruses.

check.q: The map shows weak crop in the high, sandy part of the field on a hot afternoon. What do you suspect first?
check.why: High, sandy or sloping ground often shows water stress, especially on afternoon thermal images.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Ground-truthing: checking the zones on foot
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Visit each problem zone with a plan and record what you find.
This lesson builds toward: For each problem zone on a map, you will write a ground-truthing plan and record what you find at the spot, with zone number, coordinates, what you saw, likely cause, how sure you are and photos.
Ground-truthing means going to the exact spot on the map and checking what is really there. Load the map on your phone with GPS (many free map and GIS apps can show your position on a drone map), or note the coordinates of each zone.
At each zone, look at the plants, leaves (top and underside), stems and roots, the soil and moisture, and insects. Compare with healthy plants a few metres away in a strong zone. Take clear photos and short notes.
Record findings in the same way every time: zone number, coordinates, crop and stage, what you saw, likely cause, how sure you are, and photo numbers. Good records make the next map easier to read, and they help an expert who confirms the cause.
Step by step:
- Number each zone and note its coordinates.
- Walk to it using a GPS map on your phone.
- Check plants, leaves, stems, roots, soil, moisture and insects.
- Compare with a healthy spot nearby.
- Record zone, coordinates, what you saw, likely cause, how sure, photo numbers.
Words to know:
- Ground-truthing: checking on the ground what a map or image shows.
- Coordinates: the latitude and longitude numbers that give an exact place.
Try it now: Make a ground-truthing form (on paper or in a phone spreadsheet) with these columns: zone, coordinates, crop and stage, what I saw, likely cause, how sure, photos. Fill one row for a real or example zone.
You can now plan and carry out a ground-truthing visit and record findings in a clear form.

check.q: How can you find the exact spot of a map zone when you are in the field?
options: Guess from the colour of the crop
Load the map on a phone with GPS, or note the zone's coordinates
Walk until the plants look bad
check.why: A phone showing your position on the drone map, or the zone's coordinates, takes you to the exact spot.

check.q: You reach zone 2 and find wilting maize. What do you record?
options: Zone number, coordinates, crop stage, what you saw, likely cause, how sure you are and photo numbers
check.why: Recording the same details every time makes records comparable and helps an expert confirm the cause.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Stitching photos into a map
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Turn a set of overlapping drone photos into one orthomosaic map.
This lesson builds toward: Given a set of overlapping drone photos, you will stitch them into an orthomosaic with free software and check it for holes and blur, with the photos named, backed up and the result checked.
Stitching software matches features shared by overlapping photos, works out where each was taken, and builds one map-accurate image called an orthomosaic. It can also make an elevation model (the height of the ground and crop).
Free options exist. OpenDroneMap is free, open-source software, and its WebODM interface lets you upload photos in a web browser on your own computer. There are also paid cloud services and the drone maker's own apps; check their current prices and where they store your data.
Processing needs a reasonably strong computer and time: a few hundred photos can take an hour or more. Copy the photos off the drone into a folder named with the farm, field and date, back them up, then process. Check the result: holes, blurry areas or bent rows mean the overlap or photos were poor.
Step by step:
- Copy photos to a folder named farm_field_date (for example Kitale_Block3_2026-11-04).
- Back up the folder.
- Open the stitching software and create a new task.
- Add the photos and start processing.
- Check the orthomosaic for holes, blur and bent rows.
- Export it as a GeoTIFF (a map image with location built in).
Words to know:
- Orthomosaic: one large, map-accurate picture stitched from many overlapping photos.
- GeoTIFF: an image file that carries its location on the earth, so map software can place it correctly.
- Elevation model: a map of the height of the ground or crop surface.
Official sources:
- OpenDroneMap (free, open-source drone mapping software)
Try it now: Download a free sample drone dataset (OpenDroneMap links to sample datasets) or use your own photos. Name and back up the folder, and if your computer allows, process it into an orthomosaic. If not, write each step you would follow.
You can now organise drone photos and stitch them into an orthomosaic map with free software.

check.q: Besides an orthomosaic, what else can stitching software make?
options: An elevation model of the height of the ground and crop
check.why: Stitching software can also make an elevation model showing the height of the ground and crop.

check.q: You have just landed with 400 photos. What do you do before processing?
options: Delete the blurry ones from the drone only
Copy them into a folder named with farm, field and date, and back them up
Process them straight from the drone's card
check.why: Naming the folder and backing up the photos before processing protects the data.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Making an NDVI map in QGIS
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate and colour an NDVI map from a multispectral orthomosaic in QGIS.
This lesson builds toward: Using QGIS and a multispectral orthomosaic, you will calculate and colour an NDVI map with the field boundary and ground points shown, using the formula (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red).
QGIS is free, open-source GIS software used by governments, universities and NGOs across Africa. It can open your GeoTIFF and do maths on its bands.
If your orthomosaic has red and near-infrared bands, use the Raster Calculator to compute NDVI = (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red). Then style the result with a colour ramp (for example red to green) and set the range so differences in the field stand out.
Only colour cameras? You can still make a rough greenness index from red, green and blue bands, but it is less reliable than NDVI; treat it as a guide only. Add the field boundary and your ground-truthing points as layers so the map shows exactly where the zones are.
Step by step:
- Open QGIS and add your orthomosaic GeoTIFF.
- Check which band is red and which is near-infrared.
- Open the Raster Calculator and enter (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red) using those bands.
- Style the new layer with a red-to-green colour ramp.
- Add the field boundary and ground-truthing points.
- Export a picture of the map for your report.
Words to know:
- GIS: geographic information system: software for making and analysing maps.
- Band: one layer of light in an image, such as red, green, blue or near-infrared.
- Raster: an image made of pixels, each with a value, like a drone map.
- Layer: one set of map data, such as a field boundary or points, shown on top of others.
Official sources:
- QGIS (free, open-source GIS)
- FAO GIEWS Earth Observation (NDVI and vegetation indicators)
Try it now: Install QGIS (free) and open your orthomosaic or a sample multispectral image. Calculate NDVI with the Raster Calculator, colour it, and mark three zones as points.
You can now make a coloured NDVI map in QGIS and add zones and field boundaries to it.

check.q: What can the QGIS Raster Calculator do?
options: Do maths on an image's bands, such as calculating NDVI
check.why: The Raster Calculator does maths on bands, such as (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red).

check.q: Your NDVI map looks all one colour. What do you change?
options: Set the colour ramp's range so differences in the field stand out
check.why: Styling with a colour ramp and setting the range makes differences within the field visible.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing a field action report
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page report that tells the farmer what was found and what to do next.
This lesson builds toward: After ground-truthing, you will write a one-page field action report for the farmer, with a map picture, findings, a next step for each zone and who to contact, and no pesticide advice from the map.
A map alone does not help a busy farmer. A short report turns it into action. Keep it to one page, in plain words, in the language the farmer prefers. Many farmers will read it on a basic smartphone, so a picture and a few lines work better than a long document.
Include: farm, field, date and crop stage; the map picture with numbered zones; for each zone, what you saw on the ground, the likely cause and how sure you are; the next step (for example: replant gaps, clear a drain, ask the plant clinic to confirm a disease, check the irrigation line); and who to contact.
Never recommend a pesticide or dose from a drone map. Point the farmer to an extension officer, agrovet or plant clinic for any chemical advice, and to the label for safe use. Agree when to fly again to see if the action worked.
Step by step:
- Header: farm, field, date, crop and stage.
- Map picture with numbered zones.
- For each zone: what you saw, likely cause, how sure.
- Next step for each zone and who to contact.
- Date for the next flight to check results.
Words to know:
- Action report: a short report that says what was found and what to do.
- Agrovet: a shop that sells farm inputs such as seed, fertilizer and animal medicines, often with advice.
Try it now: Final task: using your map and ground-truthing form, write the one-page action report for the farmer: header, map picture with at least three numbered zones, finding and likely cause for each, next step, contacts and the next flight date.
You can now turn drone data into a clear one-page action report a farmer can use.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Crop health map No map, or no legend and boundary. An NDVI or colour map with a legend, a colour range that shows differences, and the field boundary. Notes the NDVI formula or index used and its limits. Problem zones Fewer than three zones, or zones picked by colour alone. At least three numbered problem zones based on differences within the field. Compares the zones with an earlier map of the same field. Ground-truthing plan No plan, or only "go and look". For each zone, what to look for, with coordinates and how findings will be recorded. Names the likely causes to check at each zone from its map pattern. Action report Longer than one page, or no next steps. One page with the map, findings, likely cause, how sure, a next step per zone and who to contact. Written in the farmer's language and agrees when to fly again. Safe advice Recommends a pesticide or dose from the map. Treats patterns as clues and sends chemical questions to an extension officer, agrovet or plant clinic. Explains to the farmer why the pattern needs confirming. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the work and check it again.

check.q: How long should a field action report be?
options: Only the map with no words
check.why: A one-page report in plain words, with a map and next steps, is what a busy farmer can use.

check.q: Your map and ground check suggest a disease in zone 3. What next step do you write?
options: Ask the plant clinic or extension officer to confirm the disease
Spray a strong fungicide at double the dose
check.why: Never recommend a pesticide or dose from a map; send the farmer to an expert to confirm first.
